claims.text: Conventional casting of CoCrFeNiTi produces porous, soft, single-phase FCC material.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi powder has oxygen content above 0.5 wt% and a coarse grain structure.
The proposed route uses 40 h of high-energy milling followed by SPS at 1250 °C for 5 min under 50 MPa with a heating rate of 100 °C/min.
Processing under argon followed by cooling to 500 °C at more than 300 °C/min is an appropriate operating condition for the proposed alloy.
The proposed route will suppress porosity and produce more than 98% relative density.
The resulting microstructure will be a nanocrystalline, FCC-dominant solid solution with minor BCC and no detectable HCP phase.
The FCC matrix will have a grain size below 500 nm.
Brittle HCP formation in CoCrFeNiTi is associated with Ti-rich segregation and oxygen interstitials.
Rapid SPS heating and a short dwell suppress diffusion-controlled HCP formation and minimize oxygen uptake.
SPS pressure and severe plastic deformation from milling promote both densification and grain refinement.
Cooling faster than 300 °C/min kinetically traps metastable FCC and prevents HCP or oxide precipitation.
The processed alloy will have a Vickers hardness of 450–550 HV due to grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has hardness below 300 HV.
Keeping oxygen below 0.8 wt% prevents oxide precipitation, embrittlement, and HCP stabilization.
Exceeding 0.8 wt% oxygen can produce TiO or HCP phases despite rapid sintering.
HCP phase stability increases significantly above 1300 °C, making 1250 °C a suitable regime for FCC–BCC stability.
A Vickers test using a 10 N load and a 15 s dwell is proposed to evaluate the hardness claim.
XRD before and after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h is proposed to assess HCP formation.
Hardness below 400 HV despite grain refinement is designated as evidence against the proposed hardness mechanism.
More than 5 vol% HCP, significant TiO, or relative density below 95% is designated as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The design specifies a 10 N Vickers load, whereas the measurement is labeled HV10, which conventionally denotes a 10 kgf load (about 98.1 N), not 10 N.

The predicted hardness is explicitly attributed to both grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening, but the experiment is framed as distinguishing grain refinement from solute strengthening without a controlled variation of solute content or an otherwise specified method to separate their contributions.
